concept.shortExplanation: Everything you have taken apart now runs at once, in a real instruct-tuned model loaded into your browser. This is not a chat toy — the conversation is the instrument panel, and every response comes with the internals you have spent five worlds learning to read: the tokenisation, the next-token distribution at each step, the sampling cut, the entropy. Your job is to make the model do specific things and prove it by pointing at the numbers.
concept.ahaMoment: You can now look at any model output and say what mechanism produced it — which tokens the sampler was choosing between, how confident the distribution was, and where the answer stopped being determined by the prompt and started being determined by temperature.

modelRequirement.fallbackMessage: This is a much larger model that runs in the cloud — connect to the internet to use it. Your local model above works fully offline.
modelRequirement.loadFailureMessage: The local model could not be loaded. It is roughly 880MB and needs WebGPU — check your browser support, storage and connection, then retry. Everything from Worlds 1 to 5 still works without it.

levels.title: Drive the Distribution
levels.instructions: Complete each challenge by writing prompts and setting sampling parameters. Every challenge is verified against the real inference trace — token counts, probabilities and entropy read from the running model.

challenges.prompt: Make the model produce a response whose first token has probability above 0.9.
Make the model produce a response whose mean per-token entropy exceeds 3 bits.
Get a complete answer in under 20 generated tokens.

hints: Each challenge reads a different number off the same kind of run — check which one you're chasing (firstTokenProbability, meanEntropyBits, or generatedTokenCount) before picking a prompt for it. A setting that helps one can actively hurt another.

Temperature and prompt certainty push the same way: an unambiguous, well-known completion (a fixed phrase, a basic fact) at a low temperature is what pushes the very first token's probability past 0.9 — sampling from a narrow distribution around whatever the model already favours. For the entropy challenge, do the opposite: a genuinely open prompt at a high temperature spreads probability across many plausible next tokens.

For the token-count challenge, ask for something with a naturally short answer and say so explicitly — 'reply in one word' or 'answer with just a number' stops the model itself well under the limit, rather than relying on maxTokens to cut off a longer answer mid-sentence.

levels.title: Find the Fork
levels.instructions: Generate a response, then identify the single position where the model was least certain — the fork where sampling, not the prompt, decided the answer. Verified against the real per-step distributions.
hints: The fork is rarely the first token — the opening of a sentence is usually heavily constrained by the prompt itself. Look later, at a genuine branch point: a comma, a choice of adjective, the moment the sentence could plausibly go two different ways.

Click a token to see its real alternatives and entropy before committing. The fork is the step with the single lowest probability — equivalently, the widest real spread of alternatives — not just whichever word looks the most interesting to you.

positionTolerance is 2, so landing within two tokens of the true fork still counts, not just the exact index. Open-ended prompts ('the weather today is', 'my favourite thing about') tend to fork earlier, since the model has more genuine freedom sooner; a prompt with one obvious continuation pushes the fork later or nearly erases it.

levels.title: Local versus Cloud
levels.instructions: Same prompt, two models — the 1B running on your machine and a much larger one in the cloud. For each axis, predict whether the bigger model will score higher, then check against the measurement taken from both generation traces. The cloud toggle needs a connection; the local model does not.
hints: This is unanswerable until both models have actually run on the same prompt — the true answer for every axis only exists once a local trace and a cloud trace both exist, so run local, then run cloud, before predicting.

Read what each axis actually measures before guessing from 'bigger is smarter' intuition: verbosity is just token count, confidence is mean per-token probability, diversity is the distinct-token ratio, decisiveness is negative mean entropy — none of them are about correctness.

Verified against how the cloud proxy actually works: the cloud endpoint returns no per-token detail at all, so its trace always measures 0 for verbosity, confidence and diversity — the honest prediction for those three is 'no, the cloud model doesn't score higher,' regardless of prompt. Decisiveness is the exception: 0 beats the local model's real (negative) decisiveness in effectively every run, so that one honestly predicts 'yes.'
